overview: Angaité names an Indigenous people of Paraguay’s Chaco whose histories include the Ko’ahlvok, Koieteves and Konjanava groups. Their language belongs to the Enlhet-Enenlhet family. Industrial expansion, ranching and loss of access to land transformed community life, while families continued to build institutions and maintain their own accounts of the past.

periods.title: Expansion around Puerto Pinasco
periods.summary: Tannin production, rail transport and ranching expanded into Indigenous country. The company’s growing network of timber camps, fences and cattle properties altered movement, work and access to water.

periods.title: Land acquired for La Patria
periods.summary: The Anglican Church acquired the La Patria property in 1983. Later community life developed through villages with their own social and political autonomy, rather than a single undifferentiated settlement.

periods.title: A documented livelihood snapshot
periods.summary: The census-based community atlas records La Patria households combining cultivation, gathering, fishing, hunting and craft production. Its descriptions belong to this census period, not to a timeless account of all Angaité communities.

periods.title: Intercommunity recreation
periods.summary: An ethnographer’s account of Easter gatherings at La Patria describes football and volleyball between community teams. Recreation provided opportunities for people from different villages to meet.

periods.title: Community decisions about territory
periods.summary: The memory project recounts an October 2022 assembly, attended by a justice of the peace, that addressed occupation of community land. Its account reports a departure in January 2023 following the agreed process.

periods.title: Young people make digital records
periods.summary: Young Angaité participants at La Patria recorded and edited material from older relatives. Learning audiovisual skills became part of preserving language and environmental knowledge across generations.

sections.title: Work and the transformation of territory

items.text: Puerto Pinasco’s tannin industry depended on quebracho timber brought from inland cutting camps. Villagra’s historical study describes railways, fenced pastures and ranches extending across Indigenous country. These installations reorganized both labor and movement, while cattle occupied water sources around which Indigenous settlements had already developed.

Falling tannin prices and the company’s later break-up disrupted employment and settlement. The study follows families dispersing among ranches and moving into communities with land of their own. An industrial company’s decline therefore did not mark the disappearance of Angaité people; it changed the conditions under which families lived.

For La Patria, the 2002 census atlas lists squash, sweet potatoes, cassava, watermelon and beans among household crops. It also records fishing, hunting and gathering palm shoots and algarrobo. The combination shows cultivated food and knowledge of uncultivated environments contributing to livelihoods in this particular community.

The same record lists wool, cotton, karaguatá, palm leaves and takuara among materials used in craft production. Agriculture, beekeeping, forestry and craft work appear among occupations. These entries document several kinds of practical expertise; they do not establish that every household practiced every activity or that techniques never changed.

The Koahlvo consultation publication brought together Angaité leaders’ and community representatives’ assessments of language use. In her 2023 conference account, Ladislaa Alcaraz identifies three areas of their proposals: writing the language, recording it, and encouraging its use and wider recognition. The publication itself was written in Spanish.

At 6 de Marzo / La Patria, Félix Navarro and Herminia Rivero contributed names and traditional uses of plants to a language-recording project reported in July 2024. Their knowledge was recorded audiovisually in kovahlok. The report documents a language and cultural resource, not clinical testing of the plants.

sections.title: A new generation records its own history

items.text: In the 2024 workshops, young Angaité participants recorded mothers and grandmothers and learned to select cuts and combine images with sound. The project report notes that some no longer understood many words used by their Elders. Editing therefore involved careful listening as well as learning how to make a film.

The report distinguishes the Angaité work on medicinal-plant names from a parallel Qom group’s recording of fiber weaving. Both groups made their own material, but their projects had different subjects. This distinction preserves who contributed each form of knowledge instead of treating neighboring peoples as interchangeable.

Memorias Angaité brings together sound recordings, photographs, audiovisual material and written works about the people in Presidente Hayes. These different media can preserve voices, images and narratives alongside published history. The archive’s existence is a documented achievement in making community memory accessible; individual recordings require their own context and attribution.

sections.title: Institutions, land and the right to decide

items.text: The La Patria account describes villages with their own social and political autonomy. Its history of a territorial dispute emphasizes community assemblies as well as engagement with state courts. This is evidence of organized decision-making, rather than a story in which outside institutions were the only actors.

The project’s account includes Jacinta Barreto’s intervention at the assembly, linking respect for community decisions to earlier restrictions on hunting and gathering. Her testimony connects territorial rights with feeding families and living on the land. It is an attributed participant’s account, rather than a substitute for the complete court record.

ending.text: Angaité communities continue despite dispossession, industrial upheaval and serious pressures on language transmission. Their history includes community institutions, recording projects and efforts to regain control over territory. The map’s 1500 endpoint is a coverage boundary, not a documented date when the people ended.
